source.title: Taxonomizing local versus global structure in neural network loss landscapes
source.authors: Yaoqing Yang; Liam Hodgkinson; Ryan Theisen; Joe Zou; Joseph E. Gonzalez; K. Ramchandran; Michael W. Mahoney

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies the proportion of randomized training labels and reports test accuracy and loss-landscape measures, addressing part of V4 with its own experiments.
record.gate_note: Figure 8 reports results across randomized-label fractions. Other statements about random-label fitting in the Introduction and conclusions of original sources are cited prior work, not this study's results. The study does not report results for fully randomized labels or training time.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own training-loss and test-accuracy results for ResNet18 trained on partially randomized CIFAR-10 labels, bearing on V4 in settings that vary batch size, learning rate, and width.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. More randomized labels worsen connectivity, local Hessian measures alone do not capture data quality, and near-zero training loss can accompany worse test accuracy in poorly connected landscapes. The broader conclusion is that optimal test accuracy accompanies globally well-connected, similar models in locally flat regions.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies the fraction of corrupted labels and analyzes loss landscapes, rather than reproducing the original random-label fitting experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported noisy-label experiments vary label fraction, model width, and batch size; the text says mode connectivity worsens with more noisy labels. Figure 8e indicates Hessian trace changes slowly with noise when training loss is small.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing label corruption worsens mode connectivity while the Hessian can remain small.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label noise can degrade global loss-landscape connectivity without substantially increasing local curvature.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed widths in poorly connected landscapes with 10% label noise, near-zero-loss configurations can generalize worse than configurations with higher training loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under noisy-label training, the generalization benefit of minimizing training loss depends on landscape connectivity and optimization settings.

record.problems: The relevant test-accuracy results are figure-only in the supplied text, with no per-condition values or uncertainty reported. The experiment does not include fully randomized labels.
record.rows_left_out: None. Figure 8 also reports Hessian trace, mode connectivity, and CKA similarity, but these measures do not directly measure the behavior named in the tested claim version.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, chance test performance, and fitting under unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time and convergence slowdown as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs. Additive uniform noise on real images is a different manipulation.

The full corruption range through 100% and the chance endpoint are not tested. The supplied figure text does not establish steady test-error degradation across corruption fractions or perfect training accuracy at each fraction.
Controlled comparisons of random-label fitting and true-label generalization with versus without explicit regularization.
Temporal ordering of learning real patterns and memorizing noisy labels.

missing.what: Training-loss results with 10% randomized labels: Phase III/IV reach almost exactly zero loss, whereas Phase I/II do not. Extract separate condition groups and retain loss as the measure rather than asserting exact training accuracy.
missing.locator: Section 3.2, Training to zero loss; Figure 4b

missing.what: Figure 8e identifies configurations with training loss below 0.005 across the noisy-label experiment. Record the threshold and recover the applicable batch sizes and corruption fractions from the figure; these cannot be identified reliably from the supplied text.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's V4 limits_scope verdict based solely on unreadable figures and untested components. R1–R6 establish neither steady degradation nor its failure. Verdicts here instead use explicit training-loss statements in the text, pending extraction of the missing rows. No external sources or files were accessed.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment tests completely random labeling or reports test error at chance under that condition.
Training time or convergence slowdown as a function of corrupted-label fraction is not reported.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.

The study varies randomized-label fractions only up to 60%, and the text does not state that training error remains perfect or that test error rises steadily. Figure 8 presents the test-accuracy curve without textual values or a description of its precise progression.

The study does not compare fitting random labels with and without weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation. It notes that data augmentation makes noisy-label training harder to converge, but does not report a result for random labels.
The study does not report whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.
